Go to St. John ? Let us see what the possibilities are. You go to St. John, you go to Halifax, you go to Portland, you go to Boston, you go to New York. There are economical principles which have to be borne in mind and to which sentiment must give way. From Montreal to Portland you have to travel some 300 miles, and you have to go very little further to Boston or New York. But if you want to go down to Halifax or St. John, you have to travel 600 or 800 miles, or three times the distance. Those of you who are business men-and of course, being a lawyer, I can lay no claim to a knowledge of business principles-will tell me whether or not you are going to haul your material over a railway 800 miles to reach the seaboard to St. John, when you need only haul it BOO miles to reach the seaboard at Portland, New York or Boston.
What about the summer time ?

I am going to deal with the summer season in a moment. To go to St. John, you have to travel 800 miles.
ilr. WALLACE. No, by the Canadian Pacific Railway 480 miles.

I was speaking of the Intercolonial Railway over -which the haulage is 830 miles. Of course one deals with the Intercolonial Railway as being our national highway, and if you deal with the Canadian Pacific Railway, you are encouraging our neighbours to the south as you then go through the state of Maine.
The hon. gentleman might give us another month in Montreal for navigation.
Take a month if you like. No vessel goes out of Montreal after the 15th of November.
The 4th of December.

Very probably the hon. gentleman can give some
instances of vessels having left on the 4th of December, but in any event you have your goods in Montreal icebound say for five months in the year.
That is better.

I am willing to make every concession, and bring it down to five months in the year, how, in that period, are you going to get your goods out of Montreal. You have to send them to Portland Boston or New York. Now, what are the conditions in the summer ?

Before the hon. gentleman leaves that subject, I think that in justice to our own ports, which I am sure he does not want to disparage, he should state what the difference in ocean voyage is between Halifax and Liverpool and New York and Liverpool.

I will deal with that by-and-by, when I will show that while Montreal or Quebec is 600 miles nearer Liverpool than New York, they are two days further away, and in these days it is not the mile, but the hour that is the measure of distance. What advantage is it to be 600 miles nearer if you are two days further away.

My hon. friend is assuming that we will have always a poorer class of steamers than these other ports.
. The SOLICITOR GENERAL. Well, that lias been the case up to the present, and I am dealing with the existing facts. Let us come down now to the summer season. How does it happen that in the years 1S97, 1898 and 1899, the steamship lines charged the Montreal shipper some 2s. 6d. to 5s. a ton higher, ocean rates than they charged to shippers from Boston, New York and Philadelphia. Not only is that. the case, but I have a letter from Mr. Smith of the Canada Atlantic, who tells me that last year in Montreal the rate ruled 15 to 20 per cent higher than in Boston, Portland or New York. How then can we compete with Boston and New York, so long as we are obliged to pay 15 per cent to 20 per cent per ton higher freight for the carriage of those goods to Liverpool than is charged the American shippers ?
Give the rates from Quebec as well.

I am not discussing the rates in Quebec, but am trying to get above this parochial question of Montreal versus Quebec. I am trying to look at the question from the national and Canadian standpoint. When we get our goods to Montreal and seek to dispose of them, what do we do ? You talk about this being the national port, but when you get your goods to Montreal, where they are 430 miles nearer Liverpool, than they would

be at Boston or New York, what do we do ? You carry them from Montreal to Boston and New York 400 miles by rail, and all for the purpose of shipment from one of these ports, which is 400 miles further away from the English market. That has been the result of the present accommodations existing at Montreal. When you get your goods to Montreal, you pay freight on them to Boston or New York, which is 400 miles further away from their destination. What is the cause of that ? My hon. friend says it is the enormous insurance, and I admit that there is something in that contention. I admit that the insurance charges from Montreal are simply enormous as compared with those from New York. I have here a memo, of the charges asked on a ship of
8,000	tons during the course of last summer in order to allow that vessel to go to Montreal and make five trips during the season. Her owners were asked to pay $22,500 more for insurance on her hull and cargo than if she had gone to New York. Just fancy, $22,500 in one season on a vessel of 8,000 tons, discrimination against Montreal in favour of New York.
Mr. BICIvERDlKE. Against the St. Lawrence route.

Call it the St. Lawrence route. My hon. friend, who is in the insurance business, will probably be able to explain how this has come to pass. My hon. friend the Minister of Marine (Sir Louis Davies) pointed out very clearly that a great deal of what was said by the hon. member for St. Antoine divison (Mr. Roddick) was based, not on imperfect, but on inaccurate information. He pointed out that the insurance combine was probably interested in endeavouring to create the impression that they werd justified in charging the exorbitant rates demanded by them. But I think, after what we have heard to-day, that the insurance combine will be forced into this position, that they will have to give us reasonable rates or be made to understand that means will be found to drive them out of the business.
In addition to what the Minister of Marine and Fisheries has said, I would point out that there are certain defects with respect to our pilotage system in the St. Lawrence which require to be remedied. I do not want to deal with the pilotage between Montreal and Quebec. But with respect to the pilotage below Quebec, certain defects exists which ought to be remedied. Take this case, and I speak from some experience in connection with collision eases. No pilot's eyesight is examined unless he has had an accident or exceeds 05 years of age. Well, the greatest cause of accidents in the lower St. Lawrence has been not so much the defects of the lighting system as the defective eyesight of the pilots.
I say there is no defect that has contributed Mr. FITZPATRICK.
to the same extent to these accidents as the defective condition of the pilots' eyesight. I venture to say that there are not twenty-five per cent of the pilots frequenting the Lower St. Lawrence who have even been tested for colour-blindness, for instance, which is a most important consideration where you have coloured lights to deal with. I make the suggestion to my hon. friend so that he may see that, with respect to the pilots' eyesight particular care should be taken. Now, what is the remedy for all this ? The remedy is the improvement of the channel. Undoubtedly improvements are needed, and undoubtedly they will be made-we have the word of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries for that. And, so far as these difficulties are concerned, I think they have been grossly exaggerated and that they can be easily removed-and that in the very near future they will be fully removed. And I say that when we face the question of expenditure, we ought not to hesitate very much. We have spent millions upon canals, we have spent millions upon railways, we have pierced the Rockies, we have spanned the prairies, we have diverted rivers-we have, in a hundred ways, given hostages to fortune. Are we going to stop here ? Or, having put our hand to the plough, are we going straight on without looking to the right or to the left, with only one thought in our minds, to do what is best for Canada ? I wish to say a word more about Montreal. I know it is a delicate question, but it seems to me that it is better to understand our limitations and difficulties. It is better to take the factsi as they are stated in good faith, at all events, and if they can be contradicted let them be contradicted. But let them not be jeered at ; a jeer is no answer, a jeer is no argument. Now, what are the conditions in Montreal ? As I said a moment ago, you have leading to Montreal a channel which, at the outside, gives you twenty-seven feet of water, and I state it-
What length ?
And I state it now and here-
What length-I am asking.

Mr. Speaker,
I state it now and here, and Mr. Reford is my authority for it, and in order that the Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) should understand what I say, that a ship was prevented from leaving Montreal drawing 25 feet 4 inches of water-
But what length of channel ?
There is forty miles of channel between Montreal and Quebec to which that applies.
Very well ; now we know.

If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Tarte) knows now, he ought to have known it before. I have it from the officials of his own department, given junder oath in the case of the Arabia, of Montreal. You have twenty-seven feet of water in the channel, 300 feet wide-these controversies are unnecessary, but if provoked they must take place-you have, in addition to that, certain seasons in the year when a vessel that draws more than 25 feet 6 inches of water will not be allowed to leave Montreal, because it is considered unsafe. lYou have more than that; at a banquet in Montreal, given in the month of September last on board the Tunisian, Mr. Allan, the head of the Montreal line of steamers, told us that the biggest ship that could be brought to Montreal was the Tunisian or the Bavarian, drawing about 26 feet of water and with a gross registered tonnage of 10,000 tons. If there is any doubt about the statement I have made, I have Mr. Reford's letter here, and I have Mr. Allan's speech under my hand. So, we have the facts testified to in this manner that the channel is accessible for vessels drawing at the outside 26 feet of water-for a 27-foot channel is not navigable for a vessel drawing 27 feet, for a vessel must have 2 feet and beyond under her keel to enable her to steer
During how many months .of the year are there only 274 feet ?
I am not in a position to answer that, but I rely upon Mr. Reford's letter, which contains the statement I have made, which has been allowed to go uncontradicted all these months.

I may state immediately, because it is a very important matter, that there are only a few weeks in the year-at times two or three weeks in the year-during which there are only 274 feet. That depth of 274 feet is at low-water in October and November. During all the other months, there are 30, 32, 33 feet of water.

Of course, the hon. Minister of Public Works has a distinct advantage over me in making statements. I am necessarily limited to the knowledge I get from others, which knowledge I give to the House, that the Arabia, in the month of September, 1897, wanted to start from Montreal drawing 25 feet 4 inches of water, and the port warden refused to allow her to go, because he said there was not sufficient water to enable her to go in safety.
What month ?
September, 1897.
During exceptionally low water. And I doubt the statement, anyhow.
Oh, oh.
Let me explain. I do not doubt the statement made by my hon. friend (Mr. Fitzpatrick). But I have followed all the inquiries, and I know the case.

I am not concerned with that, what I am concerned with is the facts. I state the fact now, that the port warden of Montreal refused on the 25th of September, 1897, to allow a vessel to leave Montreal because she was drawing 25 feet 4 inches. And as the strength of a chain is the strength of the weakest link, so I say the efficiency of a channel is the efli-ciency of the shallowest and narrowest part. It is immaterial to me that you have a depth of 500 feet in one place, if you have only 20 feet in another. I have stated the facts. And I do not know what necessity there is, if the facts are so, to be so touchy about it. I am not stating the facts in order to make a case against any one or to make a case in favour of any particular place. But, in order that the defects that exist may be remedied, they must be known. If it is proposed to have a ship channel to Montreal with 33 feet of water, I will throw up my 'hat for it with the rest, if the people of Canada want it and are ready to pay for it. It does not concern me more than it concerns any other representative of the people in this House. But, I say you cannot overcome the diversion of trade from Montreal to Portland, Boston or New York, unless you equip the port of Montreal in such a fashion as to place that port on an equal footing with the others. There is no sentiment in trade ; men will go to those places where they are best served. Men wall go to Portland, Boston or New York if they get better accommodation at these points. Now, how can you get as good accommodation in Montreal as is to be found in these other ports ? The first consideration is that you Should be able to take to Montreal vessels of equal capacity with those which go to Portland, Boston or New York. And, in that connection, let me give the House a few statistics to show that the cost of freight decreases as the tonnage of the vessel "increases.
If you have got a large ship you have cheap freight. In order to prove that, let me give a few statistics. In New York, as you are aware, they are struggling with the same difficulty that we are. But 'there you do not hear of any conflict between Brooklyn and New York, there you do not hear that there is any opposition as between Brooklyn and New York. There are difficulties, but the difficulties are considered in order that they may be remedied. Let us see what is going on in New York. We find, for instance, beginning with 1871, to what extent the cost of freight has been reduced. A table which was produced before the House of Representatives in Washington

the other day shows a gradual reduction from $8.40 a ton on flour, from $6.32 a ton on wheat, from $9.60 a ton on provisions, in 1871, to $2.40 on flour, $1.92 on wheat, and $3 on provisions, in 1898. The maximum draught of vessels has increased in the same period from 21 feet in 1871, to 32 feet in 1878 ; and their maximum tonnage from 2,000 in 1871, to 12,000 in 1898. So you see that as the size of the vessel increases the cost of freight decreases. Now, there are vessels going to New York today that draw 33 feet of water ; you have got the Oceanic of 18,000 tons, and in a few days there will be the Celtic of 21,000 tons. When the Celtic was launched the other day Mr. Wolfe said this in regard to her :
We are launching a vessel of 20,000 tons, but the limit has not yet been reached. We 'will build bigger vessels in years to come.
These vessels are going to New York, are going to Boston, are going to Portland. Are you going to get them ito Montreal? Unless you can get them to Montreal, how are you going to compete with the ports to which they go now ? That is the question which the people of this country have to consider. That is a question which the people who will have to pay the money for this expenditure ought to consider at the present time.
Now, as I said, I have no desire to approach this question in a parochial spirit. I had no desire to discuss it from the stand-: point either of Montreal, or Quebec, or St. John, or Halifax. I desire to discuss this question from the standpoint of what, in my humble opinion, is the general interest of this country. Now, some time during the course of this debate Quebec was jeered at. We were told : What can you do at Quebec ? What facilities have you at Quebec ? By-and-by Quebec will have its turn. I say that hon. gentlemen need not jeer at Quebec when millions and millions of dollars of public money have been spent for the purpose of enabling vessels to go by our doors in order to proceed to Montreal. I do not blame Montreal for having done that, I admire the enterprise of Montreal for having done it ; but after having filched our purse do not jeer at us because you find no money in it.
Will the hon. gentleman be good enough to tel'l ns how much money has been spent in Quebec, now that we are discussing the whole thing ?

I am quite willing to tell the hon. gentleman how much money has been spent in Quebec, though I do not need to do so, because he knows that better than I do, and he knows the uses that were made of it better than I do.
No, I do not.
Which counties ?
Let us have that information just now.

The money that was spent at Quebec was useful at the time it was spent. Millions were spent in Quebec, I admit It, but my recollection of it is-and the only information- that I have got is that which I acquired at the time there was an investigation going on in this House-my recollection of it is that there was something like $3,000,000 or $4,000,000 spent there. But what has been the result ? It has given us a basin in Quebec which is used now to a large extent for piling lumber and coal. A part of it, no doubt, can be used by sea-going vessels ; but bear in mind that the whole of the eastern side of the basin cannot be used by vessels drawing over 27 feet of water, you cannot get near it if your vessel draws over 27 feet of water. But I can tell my hon. friend that there is a portion of Quebec upon which there was no public money spent, that is the portion along the river front which is owned by private individuals; there are three miles of river front where there is about 40 feet of water, and all that has been done by private enterprise. More than that-since I am forced to speak about Quebec, though I do not want to deal with the question -in this -manner. I thought the Minister of Public Works, like myself, would look at it from a high national standpoint, from the standpoint of the public interest. I was labouring under the impression that it was not a case of Montreal against Quebec. Why, my hon. friend lived in Quebec some years ago-

It is not a case between Montreal and Quebec.
The SOLICITOR GENERAL-and therefore, having lived in Quebec for a short time, I am sure he has been imbued somewhat with the Quebec spirit which makes us dearly love the dear old city.
It is a question of both cities.

I shall not interrupt my hon. friend when his turn comes. Now, I say this, that so far as Quebec is concerned its harbour can afford accommodation for a hundred Oceanics. They can all float side by side in the harbour of Quebec without any harm. You can put them in a dozen different places side by side in the harbour of Quebec and no harm would come to them. It is true that you can send them to Montreal if you dig a channel deep enough, or you can put them on wheels and take them up that way, if you fancy that way, you can do anything you like if -you spend money enough. More than that, the harbour of

Quebec is open at any time until tbe middle of December, and it has been open this spring since the 1st of March. Since the 1st of March small towboats and tugboats bave been plying in the harbour of Quebec, drawing material used in the construction bf the Quebec bridge, from the Louise embankment up to the Quebec bridge above Cap Rouge, and cney have been doing that in the open harbour since the 1st of March. What is to prevent a vessel going to Quebec at any time during that period ? What is to prevent a vessel going to Quebec at any time except during the months of January and February, when you have got great snow storms to contend with and these are the only obstacles to navigation in the harbour of Quebec.
Now, I say that Quebec can be made accessible at all seasons of the year, and if Quebec is accessible at all seasons of the year, and if you have at the same time a place where you can bring the largest vessels that float, realize what it means. You have got an all-the-year-round port at Quebec, you have got a port where you can bring vessels, no matter what may be their draught, you have got the advantage of deep water. Compare those advantages with the conditions existing' at Montreal where you have for five months an icebound port, where you have got only 27 feet of water at the outside limit. These are facts, Mr. Speaker, and the people of this country should consider them in determining upon what course they should adopt in the futuijp.
Now, another thing is that when you have got your goods at Quebec you have got them at a place which is GOO miles nearer Liverpool than if you had them at New York. You have GOO miles of an advantage in distance as between Quebec and New York and is it not, after all, rather a sad commentary on the conditions existing, that, as X said before, notwithstanding that geographically we are GOO miles nearer Liverpool at Quebec than they are at New York, if you are speaking of time, we are two days farther away. I say again that in our time the mile has ceased to be the measure of distance ; it has now become the hour. In these busy times you do not hear the question as to the number of miles there are between two points but the question that a man puts to himself is now : How many hours will it take me to get from one place to the other. That is the question that is put and that is the standard by which we must determine our relations with the foreign market. Now, before concluding, I cannot help repeating in another form what the hon. gentleman who preceded me said when he spoke about the marvellous resources of Canada. It is undoubted that our resources are marvellous. It is undoubted that we have been endowed with resources which wouM enable us to make
of this Dominion not only the greater half of the North American continent but that which is far more, the most prosperous half of the North American continent. Riches beyond the dreams of avarice await the coming of the labourer to woo them from the bosom of the rocks, but what avail is it to the miner that he can take material from the mine and put it at the mouth of his pit, if to carry it to the smelter the cost is prohibitive ? An hon. gentleman said a moment ago that we are fortunate in respect to electricity. Yes, we are fortunate in that respect, but, in the province of Quebec there are to-day more than one hundred rivers running waste to the sea waiting for somebody to come and harness their energy to run a hundred different industries in every corner of our land. But, those who are most concerned in this important question are the farmers of this country and especially the farmers of the North-west. They are the men who are most concerned, because, after all, of what avail is it to the farmer of the Noidh-west that he may measure his plough furrows by the mile and that when he lias reached the end, he can look over a field of golden grain extending to the horizon if he has no market where he can turn the -grain into a stream of golden coin ? He will realize in the bitterness of experience that abundance is not wealth and that men may be poor in the midst of plenty. He will realize that, this country, and posterity will hold us responsible for this, that we shall have prevented the opening of the doors which lead to probably the greatest granary in the world, the fertile plains of the North-west.

Mr. Speaker, I wish, in the first place, to compliment this House on the manner in which the transportation question has been discussed during this debate. It is not so very long since when a question such as this received but scant attention in the parliament of Canada. I remember, some seven or eight years ago, when I, with others, began to agitate the transportation problem, we received but scant courtesy for our pains, and a great many people were disposed to think that we were merely talking buncombe. To-day we have the parliament of Canada fully seized of this question, and its discussion has been characterized by a knowledge of the subject on the paid of those who have spoken which is rare even in this Chamber. I may say, Sir, in this connection, that I have never heard a clearer deliverance on this subject than the speech made this afternoon by the ex-Minister of Railways (Hon. Mr. Haggart). I believe. Sir, that the House and the country will

331 &
appreciate that speech, both for the manner in which it was delivered and the valuable information which it contained. The solution of the transportation problem is not confined to Canada alone, but to-day it is the earnest concern of all civilized nations. Some two years ago Lord Salisbury said that all the higher politics and all the diplomacy of the world now turned on the transportation question. The war In South Africa bears on the control .of the Cape to Cairo railway ; the successful policy of England in Egypt and the Chinese question of to-day turn on the question as to which nation shall control the railways which are to open up China, which are to open up India, and which are to open up Siberia. The most serious issue at present between Great Britain and the United States is that involving the contention as to who shall control the canal across the Isthmus of Nicaragua. Here in Canada the transportation question is the most important issue before our people at the present moment. Happily for us, the phase of it which we have to consider is that which concerns the peaceful development of our vast natural resources, and not that of a rivalry between armed nations for supremacy. The transportation problem has three aspects. First, that aspect of it which deals with our internal or domestic traffic ; second, that which deals with the import and export trade of the country, and, third, the national aspect pertaining to the defences of the country and the food supply of the population. Fortunately, in Canada it is only for us to consider the commercial side of the question ; the development of our domestic and of our foreign trade. The most important of these for us is that which concerns the domestic traffic of Canada. Our population want cheap local rates for passengers and freight, and it is from that point of view that I shall chiefly deal with the question to-night. First, let me say a word as regards our export trade. Canada has four great competitors to-day in her race for the supply of breadstuffs to European and Asiatic countries, and these competitors are Argentina. Australia, Russia, and our neighbour, the United States. Now, Sir, we can see at a glance that the cost of the production of the food product is about equal in all these countries, and from that point the race starts even. It costs just about as much to raise a bushel of wheat in Canada as it does in these other countries, and, therefore, the only means by which we can hope for success is that means by which we can attain a cheaper transportation of Canadian products to the point of consumption. The country which can lay its products down cheapest in the consuming market is the country which will have the greatest development, and which will make the most money out of its industry. The country which has the cheapest means of transportation is the country that will win in Mr. MACLEAN.
this keen race of competition. In Canada we have two ways of developing our trade. We can rely on our railroad system ; we have an alternative water route ; we can use both. Owing to our geographical and climatic conditions, we can alternately use-either our rail or water systems for transportation. In my opinion, Sir, Canada should be in a position to use one system as a complement of the other, and to vary that use as the seasons and the necessity of the times require. Hon. gentlemen in this House know what my position on the transportation question is, but I intend to enlarge upon it for a few moments to-night. I believe in government ownership and government control of both1 the railway and the waterway transportation systems of Canada. I have advocated for years the public ownership of the railways of this country, and I propose to apply that solution to the question now before us. A surprising thing to me is that a couple of years ago, when some of us advocated public ownership of railways, there were very few in this House to support the doctrine, but to-day all that is changed, we have a strong representation in parliament in favour of the principle, and I believe that we have the public opinion of this country on our side.
Do I understand the hon. gentleman to say that he is in favour of the government owning the waterways ?
We do own them now.
I thought our American neighbours owned them.
I do not quite understand the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Fraser).
How could we own the St. Lawrence and utilize it to the exclusion of others ?

I did not say anything about excluding others. We own and control the canals of this country. It is the first time I ever heard that the United States own them, but perhaps my hon. friend (Mr. Fraser) would give them to the United States if he had the chance. The doctrine was laid down in England many years ago that the railways of that country should be public highways, and a great mistake was made that this doctrine was not carried into practice. My contention is, that every railway in Canada should be a public highway, owned and controlled by the people, just as the waterways are owned and controlled by the people.
I was proceeding to say that the public opinion of this country is to-day in favour of the public ownership of railways. The hon. gentleman shook his head as if he doubted it. All I have to say is that I have watched the public opinion of this country, I have been in communication with

a great many people, and every day it is surprising what information comes to me of the great change which has taken place in public opinion on this question. I read in the despatches to-day that the people of Newfoundland propose to take over the Reid system of railways there. I read in the Globe yesterday of the discussion that took place in Vancouver the other night in regard to the Vancouver and Eastern Railway; and the almost unanimous opinion of that meeting was that that road should be owned by the government either of the province or the Dominion. Everywhere where government ownership has been attempted, it has been extended. There is no proposal to abandon it.
Now, what is it that I propose in regard to the railways of this country ? I believe it would pay Canada over and over to-day to assume the control and' ownership of the Canadian Pacific Railway. That road is capitalized at $65,000,000, and I believe Canada could get possession of it by guaranteeing 3i per cent or at most 4 per cent interest on the stock of the road. That would cost about $2,500,000 a year for interest, in return for which Canada would come into possession of a great transcontinental railway system, with which we could consolidate the present Intercolonial system and the Booth and Ross lines to the city of Quebec, which would be the means of giving to this country the cheapest possible transportation. Would that be an extravagant proposition for the people of Canada to undertake ? If we intend to deal with the transportation question, we must deal with it on large and broad lines; we cannot deal with it in a picayune way; and I believe that public opinion to-day would justify the government in taking over the Canadian Pacific Railway and consolidating it with the present national lines.
It has been said in this discussion in the last two days that the important part of the transportation question was how we could get to the sea, what seaports we should have, and what canals we should have. The people of the North-west, who are the great producers of food products in this country, must rely entirely on a rail system. Building these canals in the eastern portion of Canada, improving the St. Lawrence and developing the port of Montreal are very small matters to the people of the North-west. They want the cheapest possible railway transportation, and the only way to give it to them is for the government to take over the Canadian Pacific Railway and run it in the best way to develop the great North-west and to carry the food products of that portion of the country to the sea at the lowest possible rates.
If this country took over the Canadian Pacific Railway, what would it have ? It would have one of the finest assets a country could possibly have. It would have a transcontintenal system that would touch
every province of this country. It would have a system that would touch the Niagara frontier, the Detroit river, and the Georgian Bay, and would connect with the seaports of Montreal, Quebec, St. John, Halifax and any other seaports we might have in the maritime provinces. That would be a great advantage in the solution of the transportation question. What greater advantage could we have than for the state to own a great transcontinental railway that touched every province, that connected with all our seaports not only on the Atlantic but on the Pacific, and in that way give us a market on the two oceans for the enormous production of foodstuffs which Canada now has, and will have in the future in a much greater degree, in the central portion of the Dominion.
If Canada acquired control of the Canadian Pacific Railway, it would at once get back all the lands which have been granted to that company, which are needed for settlement, and which we could afford to give to settlers on much better terms than the railway company will do. That is a burning question among the people of the North-west, and that is the only solution of that question.
What does the nationalization of the Canadian Pacific Railway mean ? It means that Canada will have a national entrance into every city and seaport in Canada-something that is worth millions of money. If the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Grand Trunk Railway are to be rival roads, their resources will be frittered away in getting entrance to these cities and seaports; but with the possession of the Canadian Pacific Railway, the government would have entrance into all these cities and seaports, which would be a most important factor in giving the people cheap transportation.
If the country controlled the Canadian Pacific Railway, what would be the effect of that ? The public ownership of one great railway system would be the most effective discipline of all other roads in the country. It would discipline them in the matter of rates. The government could set the pace, and they would have to come to the government rates.
Consider also the great advantage such a national system of railways would give in building up the postal service of the country and in establishing a cheap parcel system.
Then, there is a danger to-day, which is now admitted all over the continent, of the Canadian Pacific Railway passing out of the control of Canada. Its ownership could be acquired in New York to-morrow. Mr. Shaughnessy might go to his office tomorrow at 10 o'clock, and see there an order signed by a man like Mr. Morgan of New York to the effect that the road had passed into the control of Mr. Morgan and his associates, and that they proposed to run it as a part of the United States system of railways; and perhaps they would use it to the

detriment of Canadian interests. That is a thing which could happen any day, and I believe it threatens us to-day. If that is so, it is in the public interest that Canada should take over this railway immediately.
Public ownership of the Canadian Pacific Railway would do away with one thing which is working a great injury to this country to-day. We all know how the Grand Trunk Railway, in its early days, succeeded in keeping the Canadian Pacific Railway out of the London market and retarded the construction of that road, and those who are close observers to-day know how the Canadian Pacific Railway are keeping their enterprise out of the London market, and no one knows that better than the hon. the Minister of the Interior (Hon. Mr. Sifton). If that hon. gentleman would care to give us the information in his possession. there would be no longer a scintilla of doubt on that point. This great corporation, which Canada has created at the cost of such a vast expenditure of money and such large concessions of land, is to-day a public menace to this country. It has gone out of its way to block the London market to certain men who are seeking to develop other sections of Canada by the building of railways. But in all their efforts they find themselves opposed by this corporation to which we have given such extensive powers and concessions, and I think it would be in the public interest for -this government to take over the Canadian Pacific .Railway in order to avoid a continuance of that condition of affairs. That company poses as a patriotic corporation, hut is is only patriotic when its own ends are to be served, and it can be used and the Grand Trunk Railway can be used, and both have been used on behalf of interests detrimental to Canada and to promote the building up of ports such as Portland and Boston and other American seaports. If we were Canadian and national, we would assume the control of onr own railways in order to have a greater measure of success in our competition with other food producing countries.
Take the Booth railway system, which, I have suggested, should be immediately nationalized by this government. We have heard a great deal about Lord Mount Stephen and Sir William Van Horne and Mr. Shaughnessy and Mr. Hays, and the other railway magnates in this country, but there is a man who rose from humble beginnings in this town, a gentleman by the name of Booth, who has shown greater foresight and policy than almost the whole of these other magnates put together. As a friend of mine told me this morning, he was neither bred nor born a railway man, but he has the intuition and capacity for railway organization and the ability to see where he could do something, and I believe to-day controls a railway which is a Mr. MACLEAN.
greater factor in the transportation question than any corresponding number of miles of railway on the continent. He owns the railway from Parry Sound through Ottawa to Montreal, and on to the city of New York, and arrangements can be made whereby that Parry Sound Railway can cross the Ottawa river at Hawkesbury and go on to our seaport at Quebec. And I believe that that one railway, if it were owned by the people of Canada, would give cheaper railway transportation from Lake Superior and Michigan to Quebec than any other railway in Canada. I would like to see that railway taken over by Canada at a reasonable price, and I believe that the Canadian public to-day would endorse the action of any government which would adopt such a policy and run that railway for all it is worth in the settlement of the transportation problem. Some hon. gentlemen may say that that is too big a proposition for Canada to entertain. I do not think it is. We can only settle this transportation problem by such a policy, and we must be prepared to spend large sums and not to halt, once we put our hand to the plough, but continue until we have given the country the very cheapest possible transportation.
Coming to the question of seaports, what is it we ought to do at present ? We ought to take the best possible advantage of every thing we have. What have we today ? We have improved our St. Lawrence and Welland canal system. The people of Chicago understand what that is worth, and a Chicago line of ocean steamers built in the west are about to inaugurate a through line of traffic between that city and Europe via the Canadian canal system, known as the Welland and St. Lawrence canals. Surely we ought to try and realize to the utmost the advantages of the canals we now possess, and also our advantages in connection with the harbour of Montreal, and that splendid harbour of Quebec. We are just entering on the solution of the problem of cheap transportation in this country. We have the Welland canal which has been made a 14-foot canal, and the St. Lawrence canal in connection with it, through which freight can be carried to the great port of Quebec, about which we have heard so much to-day. We believe that by utilizing these canals to their full advantage, better rates can be obtained this year than ever before. And if we would get possession of both systems of railways and straighten out the curves and lessen the gradients, we would have the cheapest possible railway transportation between the great lakes and the Atlantic seaboard.
We have besides the government system of railway which touches at Montreal and Quebec and the ports of the maritime provinces, and which can he improved in its grades and curves and double tracked at

places, and be made the complement of our canal system and the Booth line, whether we take that line over or allow it to continue in its present ownership. So that in a great many ways opportunities are presented to this government and parliament of doing something immediately for the improvement of transportation. We can utilize the port of Quebec as it is to-day, we can utilize the Intercolonial Railway, and we can complement all this by taking the Canadian Pacific Railway, and in that way secure the cheapest possible transportation for the people of the North-west. What the North-west wants is cheap transportation, and the only way to get the cheapest is for the government to acquire the ownership of the Canadian Pacific Railway.
As regards the St. Lawrence route, I do not know exactly what the policy of the government ought to be. That will require the most complete discussion. I believe that we ought to start here and now to tackle this question in the same way that a similar one has been approached in the United States. They have had for years a commission examining into a similar question which has collected a lot of information, and they are working on the lines suggested by that commission of experts. In this House to-day and at other times the proposal has been mooted that Canada should embark on the construction of the Georgian Bay ship canal, and utilize the Georgian Bay and Lake NIpissing, and the Ottawa river. That is a great proposition, involving the expenditure of many millions of dollars, and I do not know but what it is a good proposition. I believe that water transportation for the hauling of freight is the cheapest. And I am not afraid to say, that, so far as I can gather, the cheapest transportation for heavy freight, such as breadstuffs and iron ore may be by the Georgian Bay canal. To ascertain that, we must have expert testimony. It has been proposed here, and I believe it would be a good thing, that the government cannot too soon go into that question and learn what the Georgian Bay canal will do for Canada. I do not believe the western and southern portion of Ontario or any other part of the country will object to the construction of that canal, if it is shown that it will have a great effect in reducing transportation rates. Canada, when it becomes the seat of the cheapest transportation will develop, as the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals has said, tremendously. I believe that the next few years will see a marvellous development; and there will be work for every system of transportation we have in carrying the trade that will present itself.
Now, what is the main thing that has come before the House in connection with this question? It is that to succeed in relation to this transportation question, Canada must build
and own her own steamships. As far as I can gather from this debate, we are now at the mercy of the British ship-builder and shipowner. We must find a policy of building our own ships, whether for inland or ocean navigation. I do not think this House could be occupied in a better service for the next month or two than in finding some way of developing a great steel ship-building industry in Canada. We have a maritime population in our eastern provinces which is not equalled in any portion of the world. At one time our maritime provinces had a large ship-building industry and daring navigators who went to all parts of the world In search of trade. But, apparently, that has fallen away. I believe a ship-building industry could be organized and established in our maritime provinces that would at once put Canada at the head of the sea-faring nations of the world. The government are claiming credit for promoting ia isteel-rall industry in this country. But it would be of greater value-and it is a thing that should be supported by our maritime provinces and the whole country-to produce a great steel shipbuilding industry in Canada. I believe we can easily get it. We could give bounties on ship-building and we could go to one of the great shipyards in England and induce the proprietors to transport their industry and their mep to Canada. This could be done within six months.
How about the Alien Labour law ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I do not think the Alien Labour law is directed against Britishers coming into Canada.
I am with the hon. gentleman but I thought he meant
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
Not at all. When we are told that British ship-owners and insurance companies do not care to come to this country, let us be self-reliant, let us have our rights, let us have our ships, build them ourselves and take our own risks upon them, as we ought to do. We have the capital, we have the men, and we ought to have the public spirit and the administration to bring it about. If we desire to settle the transportation question, nothing can be done, to my mind, that will help in that direction so much as the encouragement of the building in this country of steel ships both for ocean and inland navigation. I would endorse any action of the government looking to the immediate construction of a small fast Atlantic service owned and controlled by this country between Canada and Great Britain. I believe we ought to translate to this country a British shipyard and workmen, engine builders and steamship designers, that would build for us out of Canadian iron say three first-class Atlantic liners, not very large, but swift and adapted to fast passenger express

service. I believe that Canada could then give the world the fastest Atlantic service possible. Two steamers would do it. The hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries shakes his head. At any rate, two steamers could make the experiment.
You would want four.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
You could start the experiment with two. If you show to the people of New York and Chicago, as well as to the people of Canada, that the fastest transatlantic service is between an eastern maritime province port and some port in Great Britain, and if you show that this service is in connection with a government system of railways which will assure passengers and mails an earlier delivery in our cities and in the western states, and even in New York, than can be had otherwise, this country would receive an advertisement and a boom the like of which it never had before. And I hope the government and this House, now that this question has been opened, will determine not only that we must improve our transportation, but that we must give the best possible railway, canal and seaport facilities. But, in order to do the very best possible for the country, we must build our own steamships, whether for inland or ocean navigation, and we must own them ourselves, and insure them ourselves if necessary. That is a patriotic policy, that is the policy that ought to commend itself to the House.
Now, I do not know that I have much further to say. I have often spoken on transportation before, I have often urged public ownership ; but the desirability of public ownership of railways never came home to my mind with such force as it does now. I desire to assure the House that, so far as I can gather, the opinion of Canada to-day is in favour of public ownership of railways and in favour of a large expenditure for the purpose of improving our canal system and our seaports, and if necessary building the Georgian Bay canal, if it will do what they say it will, and what, so far as I can see, it will do. Canada has enormous resources. What the hon. member for South Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart) said this afternoon in regard to our supplies of iron ore and food products, and in regard to Canada being the seat of the cheapest line of transportation, I believe is true. And that it will be realized within a few years. That being the case, we must take a large and progressive view of the matter and be ready to spend our money generously in obtaining the end in view. We ought to take care not to waste our money, or to waste our energy in discussing rival schemes or the claims of different places. I do not know whether Montreal is the best seaport or whether Quebec is the best. I do not care to take sides on that question or to listen to the petty view of it.

I want to see the case presented in its strongest national aspect, and perhaps in order to solve the problem we may require a commission of experts, as has been suggested in the House. But, whatever we do we ought to have faith in ourselves. We have gone along so far all right, and we ought not to be afraid to adopt a vigorous and progressive policy, and that policy, to my mind, ought to include, to a large extent, the public ownership of railways, and to include a policy for the creation of a steamship building industry in this country, fostered, if necessary, by the government. We will soon be able to hold our own with all the nations of the world, but we will never be able to do so until we depend upon ourselves, and ourselves alone. We must have a national winter port in this country. We must not depend on the United States for anything in regard to transportation. We do not know what day they will cut us off from the use of then-ports, we do not know what day they will withdraw the bonding privileges that we now have; and that being the case, we ought to devote all our energy and resources to creating a system of transportation that will be independent of everybody else, even of the mother country, relying solely on our own means, on our own energy, on our own canals, on our own ports, on our own railways, and, I trust, on our own steamships.

Mr. Speaker, I would not like this discussion to terminate without saying a word or two in regard to the transportation facilities of the Dominion of Canada. Since this matter was broached at first, we have heard a great deal that was not particularly germane to the question. We have heard a good deal said about the facilities of the St. Lawrence river and the lighthouses on Prince Edward Island, about the vessels which come up to Montreal and the vessels which come to Quebec ; but I have not heard any person say that there were not sufficient vessels coming to Montreal to take away all the products that come to that city from the western country. I did hear an expression of opinion which struck me as cheap politics, in a way, as to the rivalry that exists between Montreal and Quebec.
I do not think there should be any contest between Montreal and Quebec. They are both Canadian cities. Montreal has ' been the exporting city of Canada since I was born, at any rate, and many years prior to that; and I believe Montreal will be the commercial city of Canada after I am dead.
I do not think such a question should enter this debate at all. The great question that we have to consider is how to get the products of the west to tide water through Canadian channels. It makes no difference whether these products are shipped from Montreal or from Quebec, so far as Cana-

dians are concerned ; we want these products to reach tide water and to go to the old country through Canadian channels. The only object of this discussion should be to ascertain whether we can bring from our own North-west, and from the western states, the agricultural products, and send them to Europe through Canadian channels, or whether they must go through American channels.
Now, Sir, I would not take any sectional view in considering a question of this kind. I am quite willing to agree with the hon. member for Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart) if he can show me that the Georgian Bay canal will be the cheapest and most profitable route for bringing the products of the west down to Montreal ; if he can show me that, I will agree with him that the Georgian Bay canal should be built. But, Sir, we have already in Canada a national highway, a highway on which the government has spent about $100,000,000 ; the Welland canal and the St. Lawrence canals have cost this country about $100,000,000. They are practically completed to a 14-foot navigation. Are we to derive the benefit from that expenditure of money which this country is entitled to derive from it ? In my opinion, we should first endeavour to reap the benefit from that expenditure which we are entitled to. Now then, what is the situation at the present time ? Last year there reached the port of Buffalo from the west no less a quantity than 214,971,000 bushels of grain ; there went through the Welland canal 14,229,000 bushels of grain. How much of that went to Montreal ? There was only about 407,000 bushels of grain coming through the Welland canal that went to Montreal; the bulk that came through the Welland canal went to Ogden'sburg in American ships, and I see them passing through the canal every day in the summer time when I am at home.

Do you mean that only
407,000	bushels went through the Welland canal last year to Montreal ?
407,000 bushels went through the Welland canal directly to Montreal in ships.
A great deal more than that went to Montreal that was transhipped at Kingston.

There was about 40,000.000 bushels of grain all told went to Montreal last year, both by rail and by water. The Booth line people are talking about transporting 40,000,000 bushels of wheat. Now, Sir, is there a chance of our getting any share of that 215.000.000 bushels of grain that go to the port of Buffalo ? That grain is seeking the European market, it goes by New York, it goes by Philadelphia, it goes by Boston, but it will go by a Canadian route if we can show them a line of transportation which will carry grain as cheap or cheaper than it can be carried by
an American route. Is there any way in which that can be done ? I believe there is. Now, let us see what went through the Soo canal. There went through both the American and Canadian Soo canals, 56,603,961 bushels of grain coming from Lake Superior. Hardly a bushel of that grain went to Montreal. The freight on that grain amounted to $1,944,000 going through the Soo canal from Lake Superior. Is there any way in which this enormous traffic from the west can be brought through Canadian ports and out of which Canada may reap the benefit ? I think that a scheme is devised at present. I am quite willing to concur with hon. members from other sections of the country who believe that the harbours should be improved. The hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) thinks that the Midland harbour should be improved. I am quite prepared to agree with him that the government should devote its attention to the improving of the harbour at, Midland, to improving Depot harbour, to improving Collingwood harbour, but, Canada has expended millions of dollars on a national highway and let us exploit that highway to its legitimate extent. Let us first see what the Welland canal and the St. Lawrence canals can do in the way of bringing about the transporting of the products of the west to tide-water before we expend very much more money on the Georgian Bay canal, or on any other canal. Why are we not getting through Canadian ports more of the products of the west than we are getting to-day ? Our canal system is completed to a depth of 14 feet, and to my mind it would not be wise to make a greater depth of navigation than 14 feet. Hon. gentlemen talk about large ocean vessels going up through the Georgian Bay to Fort William and about large upper lake vessels coming down through the Welland canal to Kingston, but, Mr. Speaker, let me tell this House that you can never get these expensive vessels to take up their time going through a canal. A boat that cost $250,000 or $300,000 will not occupy its time going through a canaL The proposition of the future for the carrying trade of this country is to have a proper harbour facility at Port Colborne. Now, I am not talking about Port Colborne, simply because Port Colborne happens to be in the county of Welland.
No, no.

An hon. gentleman says no, no. I wish that to be distinctly understood. I have no more interest in the village of Port Colborne, or in the county of Welland, than I have in other parts of the Dominion of Canada. I represent the county of Welland, and I represent it and will endeavour to represent it in the interests of the people of Canada and not in the interests of the people of Port Colborne any more particularly than in the interests

of the whole people. I say that we have spent that enormous amount of money on our canal system. Now, let us carry it out to a legitimate conclusion. The government now is constructing a harbour at Port Colborne where it intends to expend a couple of million dollars. Can we hope that when that harbour is completed, we shall be able to have the traffic of the west going through our Canadian national waterway ? X believe we can, and, Sir, I believe X can suggest, even to the hon. exMinister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Haggart), a proposition in which he, with all his astuteness, would be willing to put money. We can bring grain to Port Colborne, and I am not suggesting Port Colborne as against any other Canadian port, or any other Canadian waterway, but we will talk for the moment as to the possibility of the Welland canal and of the St. Lawrence canals. We know that trade follows the lines of the least resistance. The two great elements of resistance are time and price, time made up of distance. The distance from Port Colborne to tide-water is shorter by rail, by many miles, than the distance from Buffalo to tide-water by rail. From Port Colborne to tide-water, which Is Montreal, by water, is 370 miles, while from Buffalo to New York it is 512 miles by water. A boat can go from Port Colborne to Montreal and return with a cargo in six days. A canal boat from Buffalo to New York takes ten days to go and eighteen days to come back. One boat, going from Port Colborne to Montreal with a cargo of grain, can make more money by one trip than a canal boat can make on the Erie canal in a whole season. We have the distance in our favour; we have the time in our favour. Now, let us see whether we have the price in our favour. Let us assume, which is the fact, that grain can be brought to Port Colborne as cheaply as it can be brought to Buffalo. They are the same distance from the starting point, practically; Port Colborne is perhaps twenty miles nearer than Buffalo, but they are practically on a par so far as distance is concerned. Let us see what is costs to take grain from Buffalo to tide-water and what is costs to take grain from Port Colborne to tide-water. The Erie canal boats get 3 cents a bushel from Buffalo to New York. The reports which I have here substantiate that. The railways charge from 3J cents to 4 cents, which is the lowest amount that they charge, but, supposing that they charge 3 cents a bushel, what can we do from Port Colborne to Montreal ? I submit this proposition to this House which is a practical financial suggestion which any hon. gentleman can understand. A vessel can be built which will carry 80,000 bushels of wheat, through the Welland and St. Lawrence canals. The Oregon carried 80,900 bushels through the Welland canal three years ago. Two years ago it carried 80,500 bushels.

A steam barge which will carry SO,000 bushels of grain from Port Colborne to Montreal can be built for $150,000 at the outside. That steam barge can make the round trip in five days, but we will give her six days. There are, on the average, 230 days of navigation on our canals. That would make forty trips, we will call it thirty-five trips, with 80,000 bushels of grain a trip, and there you have 2,800,000 bushels of grain, at 1 cent a bushel, carried during the summer by one boat. There is an earning power of $28,000 for the barge. I put it to any business man that $15,000 will pay the insurance, pay the running expenses, pay every fixed charge in connection with that proposition, and you then have left a profit of $13,000 on your investment. If you have the grain at Port Colborne, and the vessel to carry it to Montreal, it is the best business proposition you ever put before the public. Now, Sir, shall we reap the profit of this or shall we not ? I see no reason why we should not. We certainly have the ability, and all we want are the elevators at Port Colborne and Montreal. And, Sir, my proposition is this, however it may accord with the feelings of hon. gentlemen in this House ; my proposition is, that the government should own the elevators at Port Colborne, and the government should either own or control the elevators at Montreal. The government should not hand these elevators over to any private corporation. If the government owes money to the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal, let the government pay that money, and let the harbour commissioners build the elevators. Sir, it would be a suicidal policy for this government or for the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal, to allow Mr. Conners, of Buffalo, or Mr. Wolvin, of Duluth, to build and control elevators in Montreal and Port Colborne. We have ability enough to control them ourselves. There is no reason why we should hand over these franchises to American citizens.
Hear, hear.

If we cannot control these things ourselves, we had better go out of the business altogether. Now, Sir, the government is proceeding with harbour improvements at Port Colborne, and the next thing the government should do is to build at least two elevators there, with a capacity of one million bushels each. The elevator charge in Buffalo is half a cent a bushel, with ten days storage. We can charge the same rate at Port Colborne, and even then it will give a profit on the money invested. The railway companies own all the elevators in Buffalo ; they control the whole situation there. The only thing that makes Buffalo a good harbour is that they have deepened it and spent money on it, and the railway companies give them all facilities for quick and cheap transportation. That is what we in Canada must do. To my mind, in view of

all the money that has been expended on our canal system, Port Colborne is the place at which to develop our transportation. Hon. gentlemen may say : You are talking for Port Colborne, and you are talking for Welland, because you happen to live in Welland. Let me submit this to the House, as a financial proposition, and hon. gentlemen can reject it or accept it just in the light as it appears to them. I wish it to be distinctly understood that I am not talking about Port Colborne simply because it is Port Colborne. Port Colborne is 300 miles further from Duluth and Port William than is Midland or Collingwood or Depot Harbour. Why would vessels come to Port Colborne and unload a cargo of grain there rather than go to Midland, Duluth or Depot Harbour ? Let us see what took place last year. The freight rates on the volume of freight coming through the Sault canal last year, and going to Buffalo, amounted to $1,544,081, and the freight rates on the return cargoes on coal, and coal alone, amounted to $1,974,000. The return cargoes of coal brought in a greater freight rate to these ship-owners than did the cargoes to the east, and that, I say, is the very reason that these large boats would run to Port Colborne, as they do to Buffalo, to discharge their cargoes of grain, rather than go to Collingwood, Midland or Depot Harbour, and return unloaded. For several years past there have been 8,000,000 tons of coal per year carried from Lake Erie ports to upper lake ports. At the rate of 65 cents a ton, that would make $5,000,000 derived from the carriage of coal from Buffalo and Lake Erie ports to the west.
It is only fair to say that so far as it was carried from Lake Erie ports to American ports on the other side, that trade would not be open to Canadian vessels.

It is not fair to say that, because American vessels can bring grain from Duluth, unload it at Port Colborne, and go over to Erie, which is nearer to Port Colborne than it is to Buffalo. The bulk of these boats go to Erie in Pennsylvania. They can go across the lake to Port Colborne, which is only twenty miles, take on their load of coal, and away they go back to Superior, Duluth, and these western points. Montreal and Quebec can fight out their own battle as to which shall be the naitional port. I state here that there has never been a time when there has not been enough boats in Montreal to carry away all the products that ever came to Montreal. What the Montreal people want is to get a greater quantity of the products of the west to Montreal, and our object should be to devise some scheme for bringing that about. We should, with due and careful deliberation, exploit the canal system which we have at present in existence, and upon which this country has spent so much money. We should do everything 105
we can, legitimately, economically and wisely, to induce the transportation of the products of the west through that canal system ; and when that is exhausted, it is time enough to talk about the Georgian Bay canal. I am quite free to admit that the harbours should be improved ; I am quite willing to agree with the Minister of Public Works that the navigation of the French river should be improved ; but, before we start on the Georgian Bay canal system, let us see what we have in the canal system already in existence, which, properly managed, will carry all the products of the west. We should make our canals free. The Erie canal was made free in 1882, and it has been free ever since. Our elevator system should be put in the hands of the government, and only sufficient charged to cover the working expenses.
How much do you estimate that to be-the elevating charges at Port Colborne 1

The elevating charge at Buffalo Is 4 cent a bushed, with ten days' storage. The elevating and transhipping costs about f cent a bushel

62 or '63 cents, I think the report states. We should have at Port Colborne a system of government elevators so that vessels could go there and unload their cargoes into boats or steam barges carrying 80,000 bushels, if that is the limit a boat could carry through our canals. They could take that to Montreal, tranship it there and be back at Port Colborne in six days ; and if that proposition is carried out, you will get to Montreal the bulk of the grain grown in the North-west. As t have already said, it costs from Buffalo to New York 3 cents and over a bushel. We can carry grain from Port Colborne to Montreal at 1 cent a bushel and make money, and lots of it.
Sir, I have faith in this country. I may be too optimistic. Like the Minister of Finance, I do not believe that Canada has stopped-that the development of Canada is stayed. I believe the development of Canada has only begun. I believe we have only seen the dawning of the light, which will grow broader and wider and stronger until we have in Canada a greater development and prosperity than any other country under the sun. There is no reason why It should not be. We have a young and vigorous country.	We have resources unlimited-resources	undeveloped. AH we
want to do is to go forth and conquer the land. Let us do that energetically, do it successfully, and Canada is bound to be one of the prominent nations of this world.

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) has said that while we were talking our neighbours were acting. I do not believe that this statement is a fair or accurate one. We



have been acting. Perhaps we have not acted as quickly as we might have done ; but, all things considered, we have done fairly well for a nation of our size. I will not go very far back in history. I will refer only to what has been done during the last year. And permit me to say first that in discussing this important question of transportation, there is in my humble opinion no question of city and city. Speaking as a man who lives in Montreal and as one of the representatives of that city, I say without hesitation whatever, that I 'do not know anybody in Montreal who is not a well-wisher of our sister city of Quebec. Every time Quebec has asked for something, since this government has been in office, Montreal men have complied with the wishes of our Quebec allies. I call them allies, not enemies or opponents. They asked us for $1,000,000 for a bridge, and there was not one voice raised in Montreal against voting the money. They asked us to have the privilege of not paying interest on the bonds which they gave to the government years ago. They are now in debt to the amount of $1,500,000 for interest alone on these bonds. There lhas not been a Montreal voice which has insisted on that interest being paid. We know that the trade of Quebec has not been as prosperous as we hoped it might be, and we made up our minds not to ask for interest on those bonds. The government have practically assumed the debt of the harbour of Quebec. There has not been one voice in Montreal which has protested against that. Last year or the year before they asked us to allow them to issue privileged bonds to the amount of $300,000 to take precedence over the government bonds. We allowed them to do so without any protest. I am 'very sorry, then, that one of our Quebec friends has thought fit to make an onslaught *on the port of Montreal. I do not know that that onslaught will cause one more bushel of wheat to go to Quebec. X am not going to take the same position at all. I believe that there is a great future for the port of Quebec. The natural advantages of that port cannot be disputed. I have travelled a good deal and have never seen a better located port in the world. But it has been there for a long time. Before we were born, X believe it was there, and the trade of the country has not flowed to it. Montreal has received a great deal vaster amount of that trade. It may be nobody's fault except nature's. We have not created nature. We have only helped nature as we all can. The problem is a very simple one. Between Montreal and Quebec there is by water a distance of 160 miles. When a bushel of wheat has reached Lake Erie, it naturally looks for the shortest distance to the sea. Buffalo has been equipped in a magnificent way, and up to this date that port has received the greater amount of trade. My hon. friend, the Solicitor General, has told us that we have been calling Mr. TARTE.
Montreal the national harbour, and that Montreal has not vindicated its right to that title, and he has asked why. The answer is obvious. It is because we have not equipped the St. Lawrence route and the port of Montreal as they should be. We have not done for our national highway what it was necessary to do, and what we are doing now. How could we expect to have more trade through the Welland canal when there was not even the most humble accommodation at Port Colborne, which is the entrance to our Canadian system of canals ? How could we expect to handle freight successfully in Montreal when we provided no accommodation whatever there for it ? But we have now started on the right track, the port of Montreal is being properly equipped, and in a very successful manner indeed. I beg to take issue with the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) on that point. That hon. gentleman has spoken of clashings and differences which have retarded the progress of the work. He is mistaken. There were differences when the question came of adopting the plans, but it is impossible, in a question of that kind, that all minds should think alike. Various plans were submitted, and after a thorough discussion certain plans were adopted that are now being carried out. My hon. friend from the St. Law-renee division of Montreal (Mr. Biekerdike) said yesterday that that work would be completed in about a year. When the magnificent piers now toeing equipped in the port of Montreal and the magnificent shore wall to which these piers are attached, are completed, I do not hesitate to say that .Montreal will be fairly equipped to handle a much vaster amount of trade than we have handled so far.
A good deal has been said about the improvements carried out in the St. Lawrence river between Montreal and Quebec. My hon. friend the Solicitor General has warned the country, in a very eloquent manner Indeed, against the great expenditure that is in sight. But I am afraid he has given more attention to law than to dredging and improvements of navigable streams. I may apply the same remark to my hon. friend for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton). He has been a very successful man in the trade of logs, but when he comes to give us figures on the cost of dredging Lake St. Peter, he is lamentably astray. A man of his experience and standing should not have given the figures he submitted. He said yesterday that the deepening of Lake St. Peter would cost $4,000,000. But here are the facts. With the dredge that the Poison Iron Works are building -to-day for the Department of Public Works, and which will be completed toy the -middle of August, within two seasons, and even in less -time, Lake St. Peter will be deepened to 30 feet and widened to 500 feet. How much will it

cost a year to work that dredge ? At the outset $50,000, but let us say $00,000. For $150,000 Lake St. Peter will be deepened to 30 feet and widened to 500 feet with a turning basin. Why, then, are some of our friends trying to frighten the country with an imaginary expenditure ? I state here that with $2,000,000, or about that amount, the channel between Quebec and Montreal will be deepened to 30 feet and widened to 450 feet.
speakername: The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS (Hon. J. I. Tarte).

speechtext: Why not 600 feet ?

I would not undertake to ask from parliament more than is necessary to improve the St. Lawrence. There are difficulties in the way, but I am sure that with a channel of 400 feet in the straight parts of the dredged portion, the biggest ships would be able to come up to the city of Montreal, and in all the bends and turns there will be a width of between 500 and GOO feet.
A good deal has been said also about the expenditure that has already been incurred in deepening the channel between Quebec and Montreal. What are the figures ? Up to the 31st December, 1900, the sum of $4,805,000 was spent on that work. Out of that sum $2,725,000 has been spent by the Montreal Harbour Commissioners up to 1888. That debt was then assumed by this government, and since then, the Department of Public Works has spent $2,-
140,000	in widening and deepening the channel between Quebec and Montreal. I may say that the sum of $1,200,000 was spent by the old province of Canada and the harbour commissioners. Also, five and a half millions, or six millions at the outside, has been spent in dredging the channel between Quebec and Montreal. There is a distance of 50 miles of dredged channel between these two ports. In these 50 miles there has been a depth of 27 feet or 27i feet. The water fell very low in 1895. The Department of Public Works determined then that it was necessary to deepen the channel a little more; and the work we are carrying on to-day is to secure a depth of 30 feet at dead low water. In other words, during the months of May, June, July, August and part of September, there is an average depth of 30, 31, or 32 feet in the dredged parts of the St. Lawrence. In the other portions of the river, there is a depth of 40, 50, 60 or 70 feet. I am always surprised that our Quebec friends do not realize that their interests are intimately united with ours. If we do not manage in such a way so as to (have the trade from the west coming to the port of Montreal, we shall not have any trade at all from the west. Quebec will have its share of the trade. The size of ships is increasing year by year. We in Montreal do not expect, for instance, that, if there is a fast line, those fast ships will come every trip 105J
to the port of Montreal. We believe that the port of Quebec will be the fast line port. There will not be one man in the city or district of Montreal who will refuse to vote for the fast line because the fast steamers will stop at Quebec. We believe that what is beneficial to Quebec is beneficial to us, and we invite our Quebec friends to entertain the same broad views. There are, it seems, a certain number of our Quebec friends who would like to see the St. Lawrence blocked at Quebec. Well, if the St. Lawrence were blocked at Quebec, we should not see any more trade at Quebec than we see now. Because, as I said a moment ago, Quebec twenty-five years ago, ten years ago, five years ago, was where it is now. How is it that all the big steamers, instead of stopping at Quebec, go up to the, port of Montreal ? The reason is obvious-the trade from the lakes flows to Montreal and the big ships come inland as far as they can. That is a law which nobody can rebel against. Now, I have stated, to placate the fears of those who are afraid that we are going to ask tens of millions of dollars to deepen and widen the channel between Quebec and Montreal, that it will cost a very moderate sum of money to complete the work we are carrying on now. I must add immediately that, at the opening of the season, the Department of Public Works have six powerful dredges at work on the St. Lawrence between Quebec and Montreal. By the middle of August, the big, powerful suction dredge that is being built in Toronto will be at work. Before going further, I must endorse what my hon. friend and colleague the Minister of Marine and Fisheries has said this afternoon. He has alluded to the deepening of the north channel of the Island of Orleans. The chief engineer of the Department of Public Works has said to me over and over again, and lately to, that there is very little work- perhaps six months work-to get a depth of over 30 feet in that channel. If that can be accomplished, as I have no doubt it can, my hon. friend and colleague is right in saying that revolution will be caused.
What kind of revolution ?

It will permit ships to avoid all the difficult points that they must traverse now. The ex-Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Haggart) has dealt with great authority with the question of what he has called- improperly as many others have done-the Georgian Bay canal. Permit me to say that this is not a canal at all; it is purely and simply the improvement of a waterway, the French river and the Ottawa river. I am not prepared to say that I would endorse immediately a big scheme of improving the whole of that waterway. It would necessitate a vast expenditure of money. Of course, this country seems to be ready

to go into a large expenditure of money to secure the best possible transportation facilities. But there are limits that, perhaps, it is not well to forget.
